explain.headline: The looming crisis of world unemployment and India's demographic challenge
static: The United Nations Population Fund defines the demographic dividend as economic growth potential arising when the working-age share of the population exceeds the non-working share.
As fertility falls, working-age adults briefly outnumber dependents, lifting productivity and savings much like the East Asian economic miracle of the late 20th century.
The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 was enacted to decriminalise minor business offences and improve the ease of doing business in India.

A McKinsey Global Institute report (2023) gives India a 33-year window to use its demographic dividend, while the IMF estimates it could add nearly 2 percentage points a year to per capita GDP growth.
India's demographic window is unevenly distributed, with Southern States nearing the end of their dividend while Northern States still have expanding workforces.

texts.x: UPSC Syllabus: Gs Paper 3 – Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation, of resources, growth, development and employment. Introduction The world is approaching a major employment challenge as developing countries add a large number of young workers while job creation remains insufficient. Over the coming decade, the gap between new labour-market entrants and…
A widening jobs gap threatens the promise of demographic dividends; the Global South faces an unprecedented employment challenge

points: A World Bank forecast warns that 1.2 billion young people in the Global South will reach working age over the coming decade while the global economy will create only 400 million viable jobs.
The resulting jobs gap of about 800 million threatens to turn the demographic dividend into social instability and forced migration towards the Global North.
Traditional economic ladders like light manufacturing are stalling due to automation, robotics, and premature deindustrialisation in developing nations.
The World Bank prescribes unlocking private capital, dismantling regulatory sclerosis, and fixing costly capital, erratic rules, predatory taxation, and weak property rights.
India faces a narrow demographic window with a median age under 30, but employment has not kept pace with GDP growth.
Key constraints in India include skills mismatch, underemployment, low female labour force participation, and farming holding nearly half the population while yielding only 16% of GDP in FY24.
Only 4.4% of young Indians hold formal vocational training, a quarter of youth aged 15 to 29 are NEET, and AI threatens entry-level IT and back-office jobs.
Proposed remedies include job-linked incentives for labour-intensive sectors, expanding the care workforce, simplifying regulations, and funding childcare and safe transport for women.
sum.text:
A World Bank forecast warns that 1.2 billion young people in the Global South , the developing world, will reach working age over the coming decade. The global economy will create no more than 400 million viable jobs. The gap of about 800 million jobs threatens to turn the demographic dividend , the growth boost a young workforce can give, into instability.
Demographic dividend formula: As fertility falls, working-age adults briefly outnumber dependents, like a household with more earners than dependents. This window lifts productivity and savings.
East Asian miracle: The formula fuelled the East Asian economic miracle of the late 20th century.
Factory jobs ladder: Light manufacturing once moved unskilled workers from subsistence farming into urban jobs. Automation, robotics and industrial software have cut how much labour factories need.
Premature deindustrialisation: Developing countries now lose factory jobs before reaching the income levels at which today’s rich economies industrialised.
The takeaway: Youth bulges are arriving just as the old ladders of mobility stall, so a larger workforce no longer guarantees growth.
World Bank prescription: Unlock private capital and dismantle regulatory sclerosis , meaning rules so complex that they choke new firms.
Barriers to small firms: Costly capital, erratic rules, predatory taxation and weak property rights deter investment. So small firms, the main job creators, cannot grow and hire.
India’s record: India lags on regulation but does better on infrastructure . Building it absorbs labour, and the finished assets cut business costs.
Agri-tech and food value chains: Cold chains and local food processing can create rural jobs, so fewer people move to cities out of need ( distress migration ).
Care economy: Nursing, community health and elder-care jobs cannot be outsourced and go largely to young women .
Tourism and culture: Tourism is labour-intensive and resists automation.
Green manufacturing: Solar components and electric two-wheelers can absorb labour if paired with skill-building.
Social instability: Educated youth shut out of work lose trust in governments, which fuels polarisation, extremism and civil unrest .
Migration pressure: Joblessness in the Global South will push forced migration towards the Global North .
India’s position: The world’s most populous nation adds millions of young workers each year, with a median age under 30 . Its employment has not kept pace with GDP growth.

explain.headline: The ECI’s constitutional mandate is under strain due to Special Intensive Revision
static: Article 324 of the Constitution provides for the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to be vested in an Election Commission.
The Election Commission consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may fix.
Under the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, appointments are made by the President on the recommendation of a selection committee.
The CEC is removable from office only in the manner and on the grounds like a Supreme Court judge, ensuring high security of tenure.
Other Election Commissioners can be removed only upon the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner.
Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 governs the preparation and revision of electoral rolls.

texts.x: The Election Commission of India’s conduct raises serious questions about legality, accountability and constitutional propriety

points: The Election Commission of India faces allegations of mass voter deletion through a Special Intensive Revision that critics argue lacks a clear legal basis.
Draft Article 289 originally proposed decentralised election machinery, but Dr B.R. Ambedkar centralised it to prevent provincial governments from partisan voter deletions.
Section 21(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 permits special revisions only for specific constituencies, making a State-wide special revision contestable.
Reports indicate about 13 crore voters have been removed nationwide, conflicting with the universal adult suffrage mandate provided under Article 326.
The Chief Election Commissioner allegedly took unilateral decisions while excluding the other two Election Commissioners from crucial processes.
Opposition parties are planning an impeachment motion against the CEC, though presiding officers can disallow such motions at the threshold.
Section 16 of the 2023 Act shields the CEC and ECs from civil and criminal liability for life, creating a massive accountability gap.
The author suggests amending Section 21, mandating recorded collective commission decisions, narrowing legal immunity, and ensuring individual notice before voter deletion.
sum.text:
The Constitution placed the Election Commission of India (ECI) beyond executive control to stop partisan deletion of voters, yet the ECI now faces charges of mass deletion through a revision the law does not name. A former Secretary General of the Lok Sabha argues the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) lacks a legal basis and the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) ‘s unilateral decisions have created a constitutional crisis.
Original proposal: Draft Article 289 proposed decentralised machinery: a chief election commissioner in each province for State rolls and elections, and one at the Centre for national polls.
Why it was rejected: Provincial commissioners, mostly Chief Ministers’ nominees, had deleted voters seen as opponents. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar moved a new Article centralising the machinery “outside the control of the executive government” .
Loyalist fear: Shibban Lal Saxena feared a loyalist CEC and proposed appointment by a two-thirds parliamentary vote, like United States Senate confirmation .
The takeaway: The mass deletion of voters that drove centralisation is now alleged against the central body itself.
Ordinary revision: Section 21(2) of the Representation of the People (RP) Act, 1950 provides for revision before each general election or by-election, or in any year the ECI directs.
Method: Under Rule 25 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 , that revision may be intensive (roll prepared afresh), summary (existing roll updated), or partly both.
Special revision: Section 21(3) allows a special revision for reasons recorded, but only for “any constituency or part of a constituency” where special circumstances exist.
Limits of Article 324: Article 324 lets the ECI act where statute is silent, never against the law. Eg. Mohinder Singh Gill (1978) recognised this gap-filling power.
Scale of removal: About 13 crore voters have reportedly been removed nationwide, possibly the largest disenfranchisement exercise in any democracy.
Article 326 conflict: Article 326 provides for universal adult suffrage , so its scheme is to include eligible voters. The SIR has instead worked to exclude them.
Unilateral CEC: The two Election Commissioners (ECs) say they were excluded from crucial decisions. The author argues a decision the CEC takes alone is invalid, as is every action that follows.
Impeachment route: Opposition parties plan an impeachment motion . The CEC is removed like a Supreme Court judge, only on proved misbehaviour.

explain.headline: How Over-Regulation Stifles Higher Educational Institutions in India
static: The University Grants Commission (UGC) is a statutory body established by an Act of Parliament in 1956 for the coordination, determination, and maintenance of standards of university education.
The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) was set up in 1945 as an advisory body and given statutory status in 1987 to regulate technical education in India.
The National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) is an autonomous body funded by the UGC established in 1994 to assess and accredit higher education institutions.
The All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE) is released annually by the Ministry of Education to provide comprehensive data on the state of higher education in India.
Autonomous institutions like IITs and IIMs are created through dedicated Acts of Parliament, granting them special status and academic independence from routine regulatory bodies.
explain.what: The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan (VBSA) Bill, 2025, proposes an overarching regulatory body for higher education, sparking debate on whether excessive compliance burdens undermine institutional quality.
explain.why_in_news: The VBSA Bill, 2025 is currently under legislative review, bringing the debate over higher education regulation and institutional autonomy into focus.
explain.background: India's higher education sector has historically suffered from regulatory fragmentation across bodies like the UGC, AICTE, and NAAC, leading to overlapping rules and compliance burdens.
significance: Highlights the policy tension between bureaucratic control and academic autonomy in Indian higher education.
Examines how metrics-driven rankings and documentation demands distract educators from actual classroom teaching and research.
Provides critical perspectives on legislative efforts like the VBSA Bill, 2025 for UPSC mains answers on education governance.
prelims: India has the world's second-largest higher education system.
About 4.65 crore students were enrolled in higher education in 2026 according to AISHE and NITI Aayog.
The VBSA Bill, 2025 proposes a single overarching regulatory apparatus for higher education.
UGC Regulation 2018 sets a 40-hour working week while requiring teachers on campus for only five hours a day.
explain.mains: Critically analyze the impact of excessive external regulation on the autonomy and quality of Higher Educational Institutions in India. Discuss whether overarching bodies like the proposed VBSA can resolve systemic fragmentation.

However, excessive supervision can shift focus from teaching and research to compliance, documentation and accreditation. This can weaken internal integrity, discourage academic innovation and…

If intensive regulatory mechanisms were the real engine of quality, our most tightly regulated universities and HEIs would have been outperforming the IISc, IITs, IIMs NITs and other similar institutions.

points: The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan (VBSA) Bill, 2025, proposes a single overarching regulatory framework to replace separate higher education regulators.
The Bill's stated aims are to ensure quality, enforce minimum standards, and prevent malpractice across colleges and universities.
The core critique is that heavy external supervision creates a paper blizzard, forcing institutions to prioritize inspection files over actual teaching quality.
Contradictory UGC regulations and metrics-driven ranking systems cause a trust deficit, stifling innovation and rewarding mere compliance.
India's best performing institutions, such as the IISc, IITs, IIMs, NITs, and IISERs, operate outside these uniform regulatory formulas.
These premier institutes set their own curricula and recruitment processes, proving that intensive regulation is not the true engine of educational quality.
The article proposes shifting to a light-but-tight approach, offering graded autonomy, outcome-based inspections, and consistent regulatory rules.
sum.text:
The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan (VBSA) Bill, 2025 , now under legislative review, seeks to overhaul how Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs) are regulated in India. The live question is whether a new overarching regulator will harm the quality it claims to protect, since India’s best institutions already work outside the regulators.
What it is: The VBSA Bill, 2025 proposes a single, overarching regulatory apparatus for higher education, replacing today’s set of separate regulators. It works like one licensing office for all colleges and universities.
Why it was proposed: The Bill’s stated aims are to ensure quality and accountability , enforce minimum standards , and prevent malpractice .
What the critique says: The problem is regulation’s “governmentality” , the habit of governing through external supervision. When supervision replaces an institution’s own internal integrity , HEIs ask only what minimum must be shown on paper.
The takeaway: A stronger regulator can produce better files without producing better teaching, which is the risk the Bill must avoid.
Fear of the regulator: HEIs optimise academic work for the inspector, not for teaching. Teachers document evidence for annual self-assessment reports instead of asking what makes a class worthwhile.
Rankings over learning: University authorities track ranking and accreditation scores , not how a teacher builds students’ intellectual engagement.
‘Paper blizzard’: Institutions now produce an evidence blizzard , a flood of digital documents made for inspection. A college can meet every norm and keep perfect files, yet its students stay disengaged.
Contradictory rules: The University Grants Commission (UGC) Regulation (2018) sets norms that do not match each other: it expects a 40-hour working week ; it requires teachers on campus for only five hours a day ; clarifications issued to fix such mismatches create fresh irregularities.
clarifications issued to fix such mismatches create fresh irregularities.
Trust deficit and risk aversion: Constant surveillance and an assembly line model of work, which treats teaching like factory output, erode trust. Institutions then avoid risk, so innovation stalls and conventional mediocrity becomes the safest option.
Outside the architecture: India’s top institutions are not bound by the regulators’ uniform formulas: the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) ; the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) and Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs) ; the National…

The U.S. first invaded Iraq in 2003 to remove Saddam Hussein and eliminate non-existent weapons of mass destruction, leading to prolonged conflict and sectarian violence.
After withdrawing in 2011, U.S. forces returned in 2014 under Operation Inherent Resolve to combat the rise of Islamic State.
Iran-backed militias and allies carried out at least 600 attacks on U.S. facilities during the regional war, making the military presence unsustainable.
The 2024 withdrawal agreement set the exit timeline, transferring primary security responsibility to Iraqi Security Forces and the Kurdish Peshmerga.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi faces the challenge of disarming powerful Iranian-backed militias and bringing all weapons under state control.

Despite the military exit, the United States will continue providing targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi partners.
sum.text:
The United States invaded Iraq in 2003 to remove Saddam Hussein and eliminate alleged weapons of mass destruction (WMDs), but the intervention produced prolonged conflict, sectarian violence and stronger Iranian influence. After withdrawing in 2011, U.S. forces returned in 2014 against Islamic State. Their final departure on September 30, 2026 ends a 23-year military involvement, while leaving Iraq responsible for managing serious security challenges. The final exit raises a central question: whether Iraqi institutions can preserve security while limiting outside influence.
2003 invasion and regime change: U.S. forces invaded Iraq to topple Saddam Hussein and remove alleged weapons of mass destruction, which later proved nonexistent.
Collapse of the Ba’athist state: The destruction of Saddam’s political order weakened existing state structures and helped deepen social and sectarian divisions across Iraq.
Sectarian conflict and human cost: The rise of Shia political forces and insurgency triggered a deadly civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of Iraqis.
Growth of jihadist groups: Al-Qaeda developed a violent branch in post-war Iraq, which later transformed into Islamic State and expanded across the region.
Islamic State’s territorial rise: At its height, Islamic State controlled about one-third of Iraq and killed thousands, making its defeat a major security priority.
Heavy American losses: Operation Iraqi Freedom caused nearly 4,500 American military deaths, around twice the number recorded in the parallel Afghanistan war.
2011 withdrawal and 2014 return: U.S. forces completed their withdrawal from Iraq in 2011. The rise of Islamic State and its capture of large parts of Iraq in 2014 led the U.S. to return and support Iraqi forces against the group.
Rise of Iranian influence: Saddam’s removal ended Iraq’s role as a buffer between Iran and Arab Gulf states, allowing Tehran to expand influence through Shia parties and militias.
Popular Mobilisation Forces: Iran-backed Shia militias formed the Popular Mobilisation Forces, which developed major political and security influence inside Iraq.
Iraq as a U.S.-Iran arena: Iraq maintained close political and military relations with both powers, while its territory increasingly became a setting for their confrontation.
Soleimani’s killing and retaliation: The U.S. killing of Qasem Soleimani in Baghdad in 2020 intensified tensions, followed by repeated attacks on American bases by Iran’s allies.

sum.text:
Indian government is considering a change to the enforcement framework under the Goods and Services Tax ( GST ) Act: removing the power of tax authorities to arrest taxpayers under GST law.
The proposal is expected to be taken up for discussion at the 57th GST Council meeting on Wednesday, 7 October. The move follows months of consultations between the Centre and states amid concerns from businesses about the use of arrest provisions and alleged overreach by tax authorities, The Indian Express reported.
If approved, the change would require amendments to GST legislation. According to the report, the Centre is likely to consider introducing the required amendments during the Winter Session of Parliament.
The proposed change is not expected to mean that serious fraud or deliberate tax evasion will go without criminal action. Intentional fraud and deceit could still lead to prosecution, while arrests in such cases may be handled under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), according to the report.
GST enforcement authorities have encountered several forms of fraud since the regime was introduced. These include the use of fake identities or mule accounts to generate fraudulent transactions and claim input tax credit, issuing invoices without an underlying supply, and non-payment of GST despite collecting the tax from customers.
Central GST formations recorded 72,393 cases of GST offences between 2021-22 and 2024-25 and made 887 arrests, according to data cited by The Indian Express . Arrests made by state tax authorities are separate from this figure.
At present, Section 69 of the Central GST (CGST) Act gives the Commissioner the power to authorise an arrest in specified cases.
The provision applies to certain offences under Section 132, including supplying goods or services without an invoice with the intention to evade tax, issuing invoices without an actual supply, and fraudulently availing input tax credit. It also covers cases where tax is collected but not paid to the government for more than three months after it becomes due.
However, an arrest cannot be authorised merely on the basis of suspicion. Section 69 requires the Commissioner to have “reasons to believe” that the person has committed an offence covered by the law. This belief must be supported by credible material and evidence.

The human suffering we have witnessed this summer from droughts, fires and extreme flooding is man-made. For most business leaders, uncertainty has become boardroom weather now and is no longer the seldom interruption in otherwise cool climes. Geopolitical strain, unpredictable energy prices, stretched supply chains and more frequent extreme weather now sit inside ordinary business decisions about cost, investment and growth. In such an environment, it is tempting to think that climate and nature are something that comes later in the pecking order of urgent priorities that stare us square in the face every day. I believe it is time to reverse this order. Instability itself is what makes the case for acting now stronger and the value is more economic now than it has ever been. Three reasons stand out to motivate us to roll up our sleeves and do what’s right: 1. Ethical The consequences of a warming planet are no longer forecasts. They are in the harvest, the water table, the insurance premium and the heatwaves we have all been privy to in different parts of the world. With workable solutions already in hand, handing a large version of the problem to the next generation is not a position any of us can defend. points: The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan (VBSA) Bill, 2025 proposes to replace the UGC, AICTE and NCTE with a single apex regulatory body.
The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 15 December 2025 and referred to a 31-member Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) for review.
The core debate centers on whether a single overarching regulator will simplify governance or merely replace old red tape with new compliance paperwork.
The proposed body features three councils: a Standards Council, a Regulatory Council, and an Accreditation Council.
Legal and medical education remain outside the scope of the VBSA Bill and will continue under their own separate statutory laws.
The Bill draws its constitutional basis from Entry 66 of the Union List, which deals with coordination and standards in higher education institutions.
The government states the reform aims to reduce compliance burdens, simplify governance, and align higher education with the National Education Policy 2020.
Pending JPC reports indicate potential safeguards for federalism and autonomy, though state universities express concerns about centralisation.
Experts emphasize that structural reform must be paired with larger research funding, faculty capacity building, and student-centric financing to succeed.
sum.text:
India’s higher education system has expanded rapidly, but access to affordable, quality seats remains limited. The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan (VBSA) Bill, 2025 proposes to replace the UGC, AICTE and NCTE with a single regulator. It is under review by a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC). The debate is whether another overarching regulator will improve quality or reduce it to compliance paperwork.
Proposal: The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 15 December 2025 and referred to a 31-member JPC. It replaces the UGC, AICTE and NCTE with a single apex body, the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan. It was earlier discussed as the Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) Bill.
Three councils: The Standards Council sets minimum standards. The Regulatory Council handles regulation, coordination and global engagement. The Accreditation Council oversees accreditation.
Scope: Legal and medical education stay outside the Bill and continue under separate laws.
Constitutional basis: The Bill draws on Entry 66 of the Union List (coordination and standards in higher education). Education itself is on the Concurrent List.
Current regulators: UGC, AICTE, NAAC and NCTE together make up the existing architecture.
Stated aim: The government says it will simplify governance, reduce compliance burden and align the sector with National Education Policy 2020.
Status: Reports in July 2026 said the JPC was set to back the Bill with safeguards on autonomy and federalism. The meeting to adopt its draft report was cancelled, so the final outcome is pending.
Shortage of quality seats: Talent exceeds the number of affordable quality seats. NEET alone draws over 20 lakh candidates for far fewer MBBS seats, so competition reflects scarcity of capacity rather than of talent.
Faculty vacancies: Large vacancies at premier institutions raise teaching loads and weaken mentoring and research supervision. Expanding enrolment without faculty expands access but not quality.
Low research intensity: GERD is only about 0.64% of GDP. Funding is concentrated in elite institutions, and most state universities and colleges have little research support.
Employability gap: Rote-learning curricula leave graduates mismatched with market needs. One industry assessment (Mercer Mettl) found only 42.6% of graduates assessed were employable.
Unequal financial burden: IIT students enjoy large implicit subsidies, but comparable students elsewhere do not. Loans alone create repayment pressure.

static: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine is awarded annually by the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute in Sweden for outstanding discoveries in the life sciences.

points: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine for research on light-activated ion channels and optogenetics.
Peter Hegemann discovered the light-sensitive protein channelrhodopsin on the surface of single-cell algae called Chlamydomonas.
Georg Nagel collaborated with Hegemann to show that channelrhodopsin acts as a biological switch controlled by blue light in different cell types.
Karl Deisseroth built on these findings in 2005 to control neurons with light and successfully applied the technique in living mice brains in 2007.
This breakthrough technology, named optogenetics, allows researchers to turn individual neurons in living brains on and off using light stimuli.
Optogenetics has transformed neuroscience by enabling precise investigation of neural circuits linked to memories, feelings, behaviour, and psychiatric disorders.
Clinical researchers are also exploring whether light-sensitive proteins can help restore vision in individuals suffering from certain visual impairments.
sum.text:
A simple query about the behaviour of an algae under light stimulus has paved the way for discoveries that have revolutionised brain studies. American scientist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have received the joint Nobel Prize for their research on light-activated ion channels and optogenetics in the year 2026. According to the Nobel assembly, their discovery has allowed researchers to turn individual neurons in living brains on and off by means of light stimuli.
But who are these three scientists whose vastly differing paths converged into this single discovery?
Who Is Peter Hegemann? The Scientist Who Found the Light-Sensitive Protein in Algae
Peter Hegemann is a biophysicist from Germany working at Humboldt University of Berlin. Being born in 1954, he developed his curiosity around a very simple, yet interesting question: how does a one-cell alga called Chlamydomonas manage to feel light and move towards it? In the course of his investigations, Peter Hegemann discovered the existence of the protein called channelrhodopsin, which was located on the surface of the algal cell.
After that, he started collaborating with another German scientist, Georg Nagel and tried to find out what the protein does. Under the influence of blue light, channelrhodopsin opens a channel, and charges come inside, creating an electrical impulse.
This discovery laid a foundation for something more important – if the protein can react to light and change the behaviour of algae, why not try to use it on other cells?
Who Is Georg Nagel? The Biophysicist Who Helped Turn Light Into a Cellular Switch
Georg Nagel, a German biophysicist at the University of Würzburg, became a key part of answering that question. Working with Hegemann, Nagel showed that channelrhodopsin could make different types of cells sensitive to light. Their research demonstrated that the protein could effectively act as a biological switch controlled by blue light.
The discovery was published in the early 2000s. It meant scientists now had a way to influence electrical activity inside cells using light rather than conventional electrical stimulation. But the discovery still needed to reach the place where its potential was greatest: the brain.
Who Is Karl Deisseroth? The Neuroscientist Who Used Light to Control Brain Cells
The next advance was made by Karl Deisseroth. He is an American neuroscientist, bioengineer, and psychiatrist who studied at Stanford University.

sum.text:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries that made it possible to control nerve cells using light. Their work laid the foundation for optogenetics, a technique that allows scientists to switch individual nerve cells on or off with pulses of light. The method has transformed neuroscience by giving researchers a way to study how specific brain cells influence memories, feelings and behaviour in living animals.
The prize recognises the discovery of light-gated ion channels — proteins that can open or close in response to light and allow electrically charged particles to pass through cells. The story began with Peter Hegemann's work on Chlamydomonas, a single-celled green alga that moves towards light. Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, a light-sensitive protein on the surface of the alga.
When exposed to blue light, the protein opens a channel that allows charged particles to enter the cell, creating an electrical signal. The researchers found that cells became sensitive to light when the gene for the protein was introduced into them. That discovery provided scientists with a potential way to control the electrical activity of other cells using light.
Karl Deisseroth then took the idea into neuroscience. He introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells and showed that shining blue light on them could trigger a nerve signal. In 2005, Deisseroth published the breakthrough in nerve cells.
Two years later, he demonstrated that the technique could be used to control nerve cells in the brains of living mice. The approach became known as optogenetics. The technique has since become a widely used research tool.
Scientists can use it to activate or silence specific groups of nerve cells and study what happens as a result — something earlier methods could not do with the same precision. The Nobel Committee said optogenetics has opened a new way of understanding how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviour. Researchers are also studying whether the technique can eventually help restore sight in people with visual impairment.

New Delhi: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Monday said a new template for bilateral investment treaties is ready and is expected to get Cabinet approval soon in a bid to make it more investor-friendly. The new template, being prepared over the last one-and-a-half years, seeks to address shortcomings in the model approved in 2016 and provide sharper protection to investors from both sides, she said. India has continued negotiations on investment protection agreements even as the new template is being finalised, she said at the Munich Security Conference here.
The latest agreement, with Saudi Arabia, goes beyond the 2016 framework and incorporates elements that are more sharply focused on protecting the interests of investors from both countries, she said. India has also concluded similar agreements with the UAE, Oman and some Central Asian countries, Sitharaman said." We have a new template which will be approved shortly. But in the meanwhile, we've not halted the process.
We are negotiating with countries with a lot more of those elements which are in the new template," she said. The minister said negotiations are underway with several countries, including Canada and Russia, on bilateral investment protection agreements." If things go well, by December we should be concluding agreements with at least three more countries," she said, adding that negotiations with Canada could be concluded by December or early next year if they progress as expected. The 2016 model bilateral investment treaty had replaced an earlier framework and became the basis for India's subsequent investment treaty negotiations.
A bilateral investment treaty is an agreement between two countries to promote and protect investments made by their investors in the other's territory. Under investment protection treaties, investors can take a sovereign government to arbitration. With Outward Direct Investment (ODI) from India increasing, there is a need to ensure that domestic investors and companies investing abroad also get adequate protection.
The current framework requires a foreign investor to wait for five years before initiating a treaty-based arbitration against India. This means that if a foreign investor has a dispute with India, it should first pursue domestic remedies for five years before bringing a claim under the agreement. sum.text:
Students aged 15 - 29 years record the highest regular trip participation at 79.1 per cent in rural India and 73.3 per cent in urban India for daily commute to attend educational Institutes. The data comes from the first-ever National Household Travel Survey (NHTS) conducted between July 2025 and June 2026. The survey was carried out by the National Statistics Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), which defined a trip as travel covering a distance of more than 1 km.
"Nearly two-thirds of students aged 6 years and above undertake within-travel-day trips of at least 1 km to attend their basic course educational institution (65.6 per cent in rural areas; 68.1 per cent in urban areas)," the Ministry noted in the survey report.
Walking serves 37.0 per cent of students nationwide, buses carry 29.5 per cent, and bicycles account for 15.8 per cent. Auto-rickshaws ferry 10.5 per cent of students overall and 14.4 per cent in urban centres, while two-wheelers support 6.7 per cent nationally and 11.5 per cent in cities.
Average travel time for students stands at 23 minutes, with 87.6 per cent arriving within half an hour and 82.0 per cent departing between 7:00 AM and 10:00 AM.
Regarding workforce movements, the survey stated: "Over half of all workers aged 15 years and above perform within-travel-day trips to fixed or non-fixed workplaces (54.5 per cent rural vs. 64.1 per cent urban)." A visible gender divide marked employment travel, with 61.9 per cent of male workers commuting daily compared to 41.9 per cent of female workers.
Two-wheelers remain the predominant choice for 42.6 per cent of the workforce. Urban mass transit systems account for 5.0 per cent of worker travel nationally, but show heavy concentration in Maharashtra at 20.7 per cent, West Bengal at 16.5 per cent, and Delhi at 14.4 per cent.
Work commutes average 25 minutes, with 83.4 per cent of employees reaching work within 30 minutes and 94.9 per cent departing before 10:00 AM.
"Workers commuting to a fixed workplace spend Rs 1044 per month in urban areas and Rs 612 per month in rural areas," the survey noted. This averages out to Rs 785 per month nationwide for fixed-workplace employees, where male workers average Rs 835 monthly against Rs 533 for female workers. For students, monthly transport expenses average Rs 443 nationwide, with urban learners spending Rs 617 and rural learners spending Rs 361.

sum.text:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Nobel Prize committee announced on Monday. The three scientists were recognised for pioneering work that enabled researchers to control the activity of specific cells using light. Their discoveries have transformed neuroscience and opened new avenues for studying how the brain and nervous system function.“Optogenetics makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain.
This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries”, the the Nobel Assembly said. Their contributionDeisseroth, a 54-year-old American, Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were selected by the Nobel Assembly of Sweden's Karolinska Institute medical university and receive a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared if there are multiple winners, Reuters reported. Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, a protein with unique properties.
They found that, regardless of which type of cell the protein was introduced into, the cells became sensitive to light. Deisseroth later introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells from rats. By illuminating the cells with blue light, he was able to trigger a nerve signal.
He subsequently demonstrated that this light-controlled switch could be used to control nerve cells in the brains of living mice. explain.headline: Supreme Court Holds Subsequent Larger Bench Ruling Cannot Serve as Ground for Review
static: The power of review of the Supreme Court of India is derived from Article 137 of the Constitution, which allows it to review any judgment or order pronounced by it.
Under Order XLVII of the Supreme Court Rules, a review petition must be filed within 30 days of the judgment and is usually considered by the same bench through circulation without oral arguments.
Grounds for review are extremely narrow: discovery of new and important matter or evidence, some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or any other sufficient reason.
A larger bench consists of a greater number of judges than the bench whose decision is under reconsideration, usually formed to resolve conflicting rulings or decide substantial questions of law.
explain.what: The Supreme Court held that a later ruling by a larger bench cannot serve as a valid ground to review a previous final judgment, specifically addressing the Aadhaar Money Bill review petitions.
explain.why_in_news: The ruling came into focus through the Supreme Court's decision on review petitions linked to the Aadhaar Money Bill case.
explain.background: Under Article 137, the Supreme Court possesses the power to review its own judgments on limited grounds such as errors apparent on the face of the record.
significance: It reinforces the legal principle of finality in judicial verdicts.
It restricts the misuse of review petitions based on subsequent legal pronouncements.
It clarifies the limits of judicial review powers under Article 137 of the Constitution.
prelims: Review petitions must typically be considered by the same bench through circulation.
explain.mains: Discuss the scope and limitations of the Supreme Court's review jurisdiction under Article 137 of the Indian Constitution.

static: The Election Commission of India is an autonomous constitutional body established under Article 324 of the Constitution to ensure free and fair elections in the country.
Originally a single-member body, the Election Commission became a multi-member body with the appointment of additional Election Commissioners ahead of the 1989 general elections.

Under the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, members are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a selection committee.
The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners hold office for a term of six years or until they attain the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.
The CEC can be removed from office only through a process of impeachment similar to that of a Supreme Court judge, while other Election Commissioners can be removed on the recommendation of the CEC.

Highlighting the potential benefits of the India-EU trade agreement, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the deal could help create more jobs in labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, footwear, toys and processed goods. Many businesses in these sectors are part of the micro and small enterprise segment.
“Those are all in the micro and small medium industry segment, which are labour-intensive,” Sitharaman said, speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting, adding that greater access to the European market could generate “more exports, more jobs”.
“So when my export to a large block of nations includes these items, whether it is footwear, textile, toys, some processed material, components, they are all in the micro and small medium industry segment, which are labour-intensive,” Sitharaman added.
The Minister also mentioned that textiles, particularly, can be in the larger segment, but even then it includes a lot of workforce, particularly women.
“So when these items find access into the large market like the European Union, these are segments which are going to generate more jobs, more exports, more jobs, and therefore it's the trade deal that has actually worked in favour of jobs,” she noted.
Sitharaman said India has opened 92.5 per cent of its tariff lines, covering around 97 per cent of tariff value under the agreement. The European Union, meanwhile, has opened about 99 per cent in value terms and possibly around 97 per cent of its tariff lines.
Speaking about the India-US trade agreement, the Finance Minister said negotiations have reached a stage where it may be difficult for either side to offer further concessions. She indicated that the remaining discussions would depend on whether the two sides can find some additional room for compromise.
Sitharaman said negotiations are still underway and both sides are continuing to engage closely. However, she noted that they appear to have reached a “plateau”, beyond which further give-and-take could become difficult.
She added that the proposed agreement is still being negotiated “hard and very rigorously”. Sitharaman also pointed to the trade imbalance as an important aspect of economic relations between India and the United States.

explain.headline: Investigating officer must collect evidence, not create it: Supreme Court upholds acquittal
static: Circumstantial evidence in criminal jurisprudence requires the prosecution to establish an unbroken chain of circumstances that points unequivocally to the guilt of the accused.
The standard of proof in criminal trials is proof beyond reasonable doubt, and any missing link in circumstantial evidence benefits the accused.
The role of the investigating officer under the Code of Criminal Procedure is fair and impartial investigation aimed at discovering the truth.
The Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized that creating or fabricating evidence vitiates the trial and undermines public faith in the criminal justice system.
explain.what: The Supreme Court upheld the acquittal of a woman accused of murder, ruling that investigating officers must collect evidence rather than create it.
explain.why_in_news: The Supreme Court dismissed the State government's appeal challenging the High Court's decision to acquit the accused due to fabricated witness testimonies.
explain.background: The case involved the 2011 murder of a stepmother and half-brother in Himachal Pradesh, where the conviction relied on questionable circumstantial evidence.
significance: Reinforces the foundational principle of criminal jurisprudence that the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt without fabricated evidence.
Serves as a crucial reminder to police forces regarding the ethical and legal bounds of investigation and evidence collection.
Important for UPSC aspirants studying the role of police, criminal justice administration, and the safeguards against miscarriage of justice.
prelims: The Supreme Court bench comprised Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi.
The murders took place in Diur, Himachal Pradesh, on September 7, 2011.
The sessions court had convicted the accused under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code on November 7, 2012.
The Himachal Pradesh High Court acquitted the accused on July 28, 2014.
explain.mains: Examine the role of investigating agencies in ensuring a fair trial. Discuss how the fabrication of evidence undermines the criminal justice system in India.

The core issue was the reliability of key prosecution witnesses, specifically a taxi driver and a hotel employee who linked the accused to the crime scene.
The Supreme Court observed that the investigating officer failed to explain what prompted the police to record the statements of these two witnesses.
The Court noted that the taxi driver and hotel employee appeared to have been set up by the police to complete the chain of circumstantial evidence.
The Bench ruled that an investigating officer's role is to collect evidence and not to create it.
The Court pointed out that no blood was found inside the taxi despite claims of a bleeding injury, and no guest records were provided for the hotel stay.
Finding the prosecution's case incomplete and untrustworthy, the Supreme Court dismissed the State government's appeal against the High Court acquittal.

Anchla @ Chanchla].A Bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi found that the prosecution had failed to establish a complete chain of circumstances proving that the accused had committed the murders. In its judgment passed on October 1, the Court found that the investigating officer had failed to explain what led the police to record the statements of a taxi driver and a hotel employee, whose accounts were later used to build the case against the accused (Anchla).
The Court said that the two witnesses appeared to have been “set up” to complete the chain of circumstantial evidence against the accused.“It is well settled that the role of the investigating officer is to collect evidence and not to create one,” the Court observed. It went on to explain that when the police record the statement of a person with no apparent connection to the crime without disclosing how that person emerged during the investigation, it may raise serious doubts about whether the witness was introduced to create evidence..The case arose from the murders of the accused’s stepmother, Mithilesh Kumari, and minor half-brother, Bhupinder Singh. The house was found locked the following morning. sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 5 (PTI) The CAQM has deployed its flying squads in 34 districts across Haryana and Punjab to prevent paddy stubble burning incidents, officials said on Monday.
Flying squads will remain deployed from October to November and will provide an extensive field-level monitoring across the two states during the paddy harvesting period, they said.
In a statement, the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) said, "The flying squads will assess the ground-level situation in their respective allocated districts and coordinate closely with the concerned authorities and field-level stakeholders for prevention and control of paddy stubble burning."
The deployment covers 18 districts in Punjab, and 16 districts in Haryana. It has been structured in successive phases, with flying squads assigned to the respective districts in different deployment periods to ensure sustained field-level monitoring throughout the paddy harvesting season, the statement said.
The district-wise deployment covers Punjab’s key paddy districts: Sangrur, Tarn Taran, Firozpur, Muktsar, Bathinda, Amritsar, Moga, Mansa, Fazilka, Patiala, Ludhiana, Kapurthala, Faridkot, Barnala, Malerkotla, Gurdaspur, Jalandhar, and Fatehgarh Sahib.
In Haryana, Jind, Fatehabad, Hisar, Kaithal, Sonipat, Rohtak, Sirsa, Karnal, Palwal, Jhajjar, Kurukshetra, Ambala, Yamunanagar, Faridabad, Panipat, and Hansi will see the presence of the squads.
"The strengthened field-level mechanism is aimed at ensuring timely assessment of on-ground situation, close coordination among enforcement agencies and prompt preventive action to tackle stubble burning incidents during the harvesting season" the CAQM added. PTI ALC

points: India launched Samudra Manthan, the National Offshore Exploration Scheme, approved on 31 July 2026, with a Phase-I financial outlay of ₹84,084 crore up to FY 2030-31.
The mission addresses heavy import dependence, high crude oil import bills of USD 144 billion, and natural production declines of 6 to 7 percent in mature fields.
The core issue tackles high financial risks and capital-intensive nature of deepwater drilling, where a single well costs between USD 125 million and USD 150 million.
Component one allocates ₹28,534 crore for extensive 2D and 3D seismic surveys, deploying AI and reprocessing older datasets via the National Data Repository.
Component two allocates ₹43,200 crore to support drilling 60 deepwater and ultra-deepwater exploration wells, providing financial assistance of up to 50 percent or ₹675 crore per well.
Component three earmarks ₹10,000 crore for shared offshore infrastructure in selected basins like Mahanadi and Kutch to make stranded discoveries commercially viable.
Component four establishes an Oil and Gas Manufacturing and Services Zone with ₹2,000 crore to strengthen domestic industrial capabilities and reduce imported equipment dependence.
An additional ₹350 crore supports programme monitoring, digital interventions, capacity building, and awareness campaigns.
The mission aims to add over 600 MMTOE to hydrocarbon reserves, increase annual domestic production to nearly 80 MMTOE, and reduce the annual import bill by ₹1 lakh crore.
sum.text:
India has launched an ambitious national mission to transform its offshore hydrocarbon exploration sector with the approval of Samudra Manthan – the National Offshore Exploration Scheme, a flagship initiative aimed at enhancing domestic oil and gas production, reducing import dependence and strengthening the country’s long-term energy security.
Approved on 31 July 2026, the scheme marks a major shift from policy reforms to mission-mode implementation. With a Phase-I financial outlay of ₹84,084 crore up to FY 2030-31, Samudra Manthan seeks to unlock India’s vast offshore hydrocarbon resources through advanced exploration technologies, large-scale seismic surveys, deepwater drilling, common offshore infrastructure and domestic manufacturing capabilities.
The initiative is designed to add more than 600 Million Metric Tonnes of Oil Equivalent (MMTOE) to the country’s hydrocarbon reserves while creating a globally competitive offshore energy ecosystem that supports the objectives of Atmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India.
As one of the world’s fastest-growing economies, India faces rapidly increasing energy demand across households, agriculture, transportation and industry. However, a substantial portion of the country’s crude oil and natural gas requirements continues to be met through imports, making energy security an important national priority.
According to the government, India’s annual crude oil import bill stands at nearly USD 144 billion, or around ₹13 lakh crore, highlighting the need to significantly enhance domestic production and reduce dependence on overseas supplies.
Hydrocarbons, which include crude oil and natural gas, form the backbone of India’s energy economy. These resources provide fuel for transportation, cooking gas, fertilisers, petrochemicals and numerous industrial products.
While considerable exploration has taken place onshore, much of India’s untapped hydrocarbon potential lies beneath the sea. Offshore basins along the country’s eastern and western coasts extend into water depths of nearly 3,000 metres and are estimated to contain more than 5,600 MMTOE of hydrocarbon resources. Recent discoveries in the Cauvery, Mahanadi and Andaman basins have further reinforced the potential of India’s offshore reserves.

Rahul Gandhi alleged on X that the CEC unilaterally changed Form 6, citing a recent Supreme Court observation.
The core issue involves the legality of an added declaration during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in Bihar.
The EC clarified that Form 6 itself was not altered, but a separate declaration seeking parents' details was attached for the Bihar SIR.
The Bihar SIR order was issued on June 24, 2025, with the unanimous approval of the Commission.
The poll panel cited a Supreme Court judgment dated May 27, 2026, and its own Press Note No. 120 dated September 26, 2026.

sum.text:
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Monday issued a “fact check” amid the controversy over reported changes to Form 6, calling Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s claim that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had “changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally” misleading. In its response, the EC said the order for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Bihar, issued on June 24, 2025, had received the unanimous approval of the Commission and was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court in its judgment dated May 27, 2026. The poll panel also cited its Press Note No. 120 dated September 26, 2026, pointing to point 1(iii), which states: “The declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.” The EC's response came after Rahul alleged in a post on X that the CEC had changed Form 6 “illegally and unilaterally”, citing the recent Supreme Court observation.
EC officials also clarified that Form 6 itself had not been changed, but that a declaration had been attached to the form under the Bihar SIR order, as quoted by PTI.The clarification came after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modification to Form 6 used by the EC during the SIR exercise in various states.“Any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us. When records are produced, we would like to see who has modified it,” a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said. Form 6 is the application used by eligible voters for inclusion in the electoral roll.
The declaration was attached to Form 6 during the Bihar SIR, which began with the EC's June 24, 2025 order. The declaration sought additional details, including information about the applicant's parents. According to EC officials, the form itself remained unchanged, while the declaration was a separate document attached to it for the SIR exercise.
Outside SIR, the forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 apply. The declaration was later withdrawn from the EC's online portals. The online version of Form 6 and the declaration also used a single OTP for both, rather than requiring separate OTP verification, which had led to suggestions that the declaration was part of Form 6.
The EC also rejected claims that it had withdrawn its September 26 press note and shared the document to show that it remained available. Get the latest India News and Live updates.

Maharashtra Water Resources Minister Girish Mahajan has directed all urban local bodies to implement a minimum 10% water cut from October 16 amid concerns over limited water reserves and reduced rainfall linked to El Niño.

Joint teams of the Revenue, Police and Water Resources departments will take action against unauthorised water withdrawal from dams, rivers and canals, Mahajan said.

static: Legislative privileges in India refer to the special rights and immunities enjoyed by Houses of Parliament and state legislatures, and their members, to function effectively.
Article 105 of the Constitution deals with the powers and privileges of Parliament, while Article 194 deals with the powers, privileges, and immunities of State Legislatures and their members.

Under Articles 105(3) and 194(3), the powers and privileges of legislatures are equivalent to those of the British House of Commons as it stood at the commencement of the Constitution, unless defined otherwise by law.

Fundamental rights, guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution including freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), often come into tension with parliamentary or legislative privileges.

The Supreme Court has previously held in landmark rulings like Raja Ram Pal v. Honble Speaker, Lok Sabha that legislative proceedings are subject to judicial review if they are unconstitutional or grossly illegal.

During the latest hearing, senior advocate Raju Ramachandran, representing the TN Assembly, stated that the withdrawal in 2004 was not brought on record earlier.

sum.text:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday indicated that its seven-judge Constitution Bench may not decide the long-pending question of whether legislative privileges can override the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression after the Tamil Nadu Assembly informed it that the disputed 2003 resolution had been withdrawn in 2004. The development came in the case concerning journalists N Ravi and others, who approached the Supreme Court after then Tamil Nadu Assembly Speaker K Kalimuthu ordered the arrest of six journalists for alleged breach of privilege and contempt following a resolution passed by the House in 2003. The apex court stayed the arrests and later referred the matter for an authoritative determination of the scope of legislative privileges.
A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was told by senior advocate Raju Ramachandran, appearing for the TN Assembly on Monday, that the 2003 resolution had been withdrawn by the House in 2004. He said the development may not have been brought on record earlier. Chief Justice Kant said the court should not engage in an “academic exercise” and stressed the need for a live controversy.

New Delhi [India], October 5 (ANI): India and Canada are set to begin the fifth round of negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) in Ottawa, with Canada pitching energy, critical minerals and aerospace cooperation as key areas for expanding economic ties between the two countries. Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said the negotiations would build on the momentum from his recent visit to Mumbai and discussions with Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal at the G20 Trade Ministers Meeting. “Tomorrow morning in Ottawa, Canada and India begin Round 5 of CEPA trade negotiations,” Sidhu said in a post on X, adding that Canada was focused on concluding a trade agreement that would “open new doors for Canadian businesses and workers in one of the world's largest economies.” The latest round follows Sidhu’s meeting with Goyal in Mumbai, where the two sides discussed the fourth round of negotiations. In his remarks at the G20 meeting, Sidhu had said India and Canada were targeting an increase in bilateral trade from USD 30 billion to USD 70 billion over the next five years. Sidhu also highlighted Canada’s potential role in meeting India’s future energy requirements, saying India’s economy is growing 7 per cent annually and its energy needs are expected to rise 70 per cent by 2035.
“Canada is ready to deliver,” Sidhu said in the post, pointing to the USD 33 billion investment in LNG Canada Phase 2. He said the project would make it the second-largest facility of its kind in the world and that Canada would become a top-five LNG exporter within five years. Beyond energy, Sidhu identified critical minerals and aerospace as other areas where Canada wants to deepen cooperation with India. He said Canada was seeking to be “the reliable partner India needs” as the two countries work towards a trade agreement. At the G20 meeting, Sidhu had also highlighted supply chain diversification as an important area of cooperation, particularly in critical minerals. He said the two countries could work together across energy, critical minerals, aerospace, investment and research. The two governments have committed to concluding the CEPA negotiations by the end of 2026, as they seek to deepen trade and investment ties and work towards their longer-term trade ambitions. Koraput (Odisha), Oct 5 (PTI) Defence Minister Rajnath Singh is scheduled to lay the foundation stone for new facilities linked to the Shakti engine at the Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) in Odisha's Koraput district on October 6, officials said on Monday.
According to official sources, Singh is likely to reach Sunabeda in the district on Tuesday afternoon after attending programmes at Hindustan Shipyard Limited in Visakhapatnam, where he is scheduled to inaugurate upgraded maritime infrastructure and participate in key shipbuilding milestones.
HAL’s Koraput division has been playing a key role in India’s military engine manufacturing and overhaul ecosystem for decades, and the Shakti engine programme is expected to give a boost to the effort, an official said on Monday.
The proposed facilities are significant for the country's efforts to strengthen its domestic capabilities in aero-engine technology and reduce import dependence, officials said.

HAL’s Koraput division was established in the 1960s and has evolved over the decades from servicing Soviet-origin aircraft engines to undertaking the manufacturing, overhaul and maintenance of engines used in modern combat aircraft.
